title: Correlation
description: Class 11 Economics: meaning and types of correlation, the scatter diagram, Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation and Spearman's rank correlation, with worked examples and interpretation.

topics.title: Meaning, Types and the Scatter Diagram
topics.concept:
In economics, two quantities often move together — for example, as the price of a good rises, its demand falls; as income rises, saving rises. Correlation measures the relationship between two variables: whether they move together, and how closely. It does not prove that one causes the other; it only shows that they are related.

Correlation can be of these types:

  • Positive correlation — the two variables move in the same direction (both rise together or both fall together), e.g. income and consumption.
  • Negative correlation — the two move in opposite directions (one rises as the other falls), e.g. price and demand.
  • Zero (no) correlation — no clear relationship.

The simplest way to see correlation is a scatter diagram — we plot each pair of values as a dot on a graph (one variable on each axis). The pattern of dots reveals the relationship: dots rising from left to right show positive correlation; dots falling from left to right show negative correlation; scattered dots with no pattern show no correlation. The more closely the dots cluster around a straight line, the stronger the correlation.

examples.problem: Example 1: Is the correlation between price and demand positive or negative? Why?
examples.solution:
They move oppositely.

  • As price rises, demand usually falls.
  • Opposite directions → negative correlation.
examples.answer: Negative correlation, because as price rises, demand falls (opposite directions).

examples.problem: Example 2: On a scatter diagram, what pattern shows positive correlation?
examples.solution:
Look at the slope of the dots.

  • Dots rising from the lower-left to the upper-right show positive correlation.
examples.answer: Dots rising from left to right (lower-left to upper-right) show positive correlation.

examples.problem: Example 3: Does correlation prove that one variable causes the other?
examples.solution:
Correlation is not causation.

  • No. Correlation only shows that two variables are related/move together.
  • It does not prove cause and effect.
examples.answer: No — correlation shows a relationship between variables but does not prove that one causes the other.

recap:
• Correlation measures the relationship between two variables (not causation).
  • Types: positive (same direction), negative (opposite), zero (no relation).
  • Scatter diagram: dots rising → positive; falling → negative; no pattern → none. Closer to a line = stronger.

quiz.q: When two variables move in the same direction, the correlation is:
quiz.explanation: Moving in the same direction is positive correlation.
Correlation shows a relationship, not causation.

topics.title: Karl Pearson's Coefficient of Correlation
topics.concept:
A scatter diagram shows the direction of correlation but not its exact strength. For an exact numerical measure we use Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation (r). Using deviations from the mean (dx = X − X̄, dy = Y − Ȳ), the formula is:

r = Σ(dx·dy) ÷ √(Σdx² × Σdy²)

The value of r always lies between −1 and +1:

  • r = +1 → perfect positive correlation.
  • r = −1 → perfect negative correlation.
  • r = 0 → no correlation.
  • Values near ±1 mean strong correlation; values near 0 mean weak correlation.

Worked example. Find r for X: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and Y: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100.

  • Means: X̄ = 150÷5 = 30; Ȳ = 300÷5 = 60.
  • dx: −20, −10, 0, 10, 20. dy: −40, −20, 0, 20, 40.
  • Σ(dx·dy) = 800 + 200 + 0 + 200 + 800 = 2000.
  • Σdx² = 400 + 100 + 0 + 100 + 400 = 1000; Σdy² = 1600 + 400 + 0 + 400 + 1600 = 4000.
  • r = 2000 ÷ √(1000 × 4000) = 2000 ÷ √4000000 = 2000 ÷ 2000 = +1.

So X and Y have perfect positive correlation — here Y is always exactly twice X. Pearson's r is the most widely used measure, but it assumes a linear relationship and (unlike the median) is affected by extreme values.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the range of Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation, and what does r = −1 mean?
examples.solution:
r is bounded.

  • r lies between −1 and +1.
  • r = −1 means perfect negative correlation.
examples.answer: r lies between −1 and +1; r = −1 means perfect negative correlation.

examples.problem: Example 2: If Σ(dx·dy) = 120, Σdx² = 100 and Σdy² = 144, find r.
Example 3: A coefficient of r = 0.15 indicates what kind of correlation?
examples.solution:
Compare with the limits.

  • 0.15 is positive but close to 0.
  • So it is a weak positive correlation.
examples.answer: A weak positive correlation (positive but near zero).

recap:
• Karl Pearson's r = Σ(dx·dy) ÷ √(Σdx² × Σdy²); dx = X−X̄, dy = Y−Ȳ.
  • Always between −1 and +1: +1 perfect positive, −1 perfect negative, 0 none.
  • Assumes a linear relation; affected by extreme values.

topics.title: Spearman's Rank Correlation and Interpretation
topics.concept:
Sometimes data cannot be measured in exact numbers but can be ranked — for example, the ranking of contestants by two judges, or items rated by beauty, honesty or efficiency. For such qualitative or ranked data we use Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (R):

R = 1 − [ 6ΣD² ÷ N(N² − 1) ]

where D is the difference between the two ranks of each item and N is the number of items. Like Pearson's r, R also lies between −1 and +1.

Worked example. Two judges rank 5 paintings as follows — Judge A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and Judge B: 2, 1, 4, 3, 5. Find the rank correlation.

  • Differences D = A − B: −1, 1, −1, 1, 0.
  • D²: 1, 1, 1, 1, 0; ΣD² = 4. N = 5, so N(N² − 1) = 5 × (25 − 1) = 5 × 24 = 120.
  • R = 1 − (6 × 4) ÷ 120 = 1 − 24÷120 = 1 − 0.2 = +0.8.

So the two judges' rankings have a high positive agreement (R = +0.8). Interpreting a correlation coefficient: a value close to +1 means a strong direct relationship, close to −1 a strong inverse relationship, and close to 0 a weak or no relationship. But always remember the golden caution: correlation is not causation — a high correlation between two things (like ice-cream sales and drowning) may be due to a third common factor (summer heat), not because one causes the other.

examples.problem: Example 1: When is Spearman's rank correlation used instead of Karl Pearson's?
examples.solution:
Think about the type of data.

  • When data are qualitative or given as ranks (e.g. ranked by judges, beauty, honesty).
examples.answer: When the data are qualitative or in the form of ranks rather than exact measurements.

examples.problem: Example 2: Find R if ΣD² = 10 and N = 5.
Example 3: Ice-cream sales and cases of drowning both rise in summer, giving a high positive correlation. Does ice cream cause drowning?
examples.solution:
Watch for a hidden third factor.

  • No. Both are caused by a third factor — hot weather.
  • Correlation is not causation.
examples.answer: No. Both are caused by a third factor (summer heat); correlation does not prove causation.

recap:
• Spearman's R = 1 − [6ΣD² ÷ N(N²−1)]; used for ranked / qualitative data; lies between −1 and +1.
  • D = difference of the two ranks; N = number of items.
  • Interpret: near +1 strong direct, near −1 strong inverse, near 0 weak/none.
  • Golden rule: correlation is not causation (beware a hidden third factor).

options: A third common factor may cause both
quiz.explanation: A hidden third factor can create correlation without causation.

questions.q: As a household's income rises, its consumption also rises. The correlation between income and consumption is:
questions.explanation: Both move in the same direction, so the correlation is positive.

questions.q: A scatter diagram whose dots lie almost exactly on an upward straight line indicates:
questions.explanation: The closer the dots hug an upward line, the nearer r is to +1.

questions.q: For data where Σ(dx·dy) is negative while Σdx² and Σdy² are positive, the value of r is:
questions.explanation: The denominator is always positive, so the sign of r follows the sign of Σ(dx·dy).

questions.q: Two examiners rank 5 students and get ΣD² = 0. The rank correlation R is:
questions.explanation: R = 1 − (6×0)/(5×24) = 1 − 0 = +1 — the examiners agree perfectly.

questions.q: Spearman's method is chosen over Pearson's when the data are about qualities like beauty or honesty because such qualities can only be:
questions.explanation: Qualities have no exact numerical scale, so we rank them and use Spearman's R.

questions.q: The number of umbrellas sold and the amount of rainfall show high positive correlation. The most likely reason is:
options: Rain genuinely drives umbrella sales (a real relationship)
questions.explanation: Here the link is real and causal — but the chapter still warns that correlation alone does not, by itself, prove causation.

questions.q: An r of −0.92 between two variables means they are:
questions.explanation: A value close to −1 shows a strong inverse (negative) relationship.

questions.q: Karl Pearson's r can be distorted by extreme values because it is based on:
questions.explanation: Because r uses the mean, an extreme value (which shifts the mean) can distort r.

questions.q: If two judges rank items in exactly the opposite order, the rank correlation R will be:
questions.explanation: Completely reversed rankings give perfect negative agreement, R = −1.

questions.q: A scatter of dots with no upward or downward pattern indicates that r is close to:
questions.explanation: No pattern means no correlation, so r is near 0.
